cards.title: Four psychological pillars of scroll-stopping Meta ads
cards.summary: Every strong ad must earn attention, open a curiosity gap, trigger an emotion, and signal connection to a specific buyer.
cards.use_when: Drafting or reviewing a new paid social creative for a product launch or existing SKU on Meta.
steps: Before writing anything, walk your concept through the four pillars: (1) Attention — grab it in the first half-second, not the widely cited three seconds; scrolling users leave faster than a second. (2) Curiosity — open a gap, especially if the ad routes to a quiz, listicle, or solid landing page that finishes the sell. You do not need to close the sale inside the ad. (3) Emotion — pick one core feeling (fear, insecurity, excitement, humor) matched to where the buyer is emotionally. (4) Connection — use the ICP's own language, slang, and in-jokes so it reads as 'made for me'.

Treat the pillars as a checklist, not a sequence: ads can lean hard on curiosity/emotion (dark problem-solving brands) or on attention/connection (light, meme-style product ads) — neither is universally correct.
Verify pillar fit by asking whether your ICP would stop on this ad versus scrolling past in two seconds; wrong-ICP ads fail regardless of production quality.
caveats: The 'half-second attention' claim is the presenter's opinion, not a benchmark; treat it as a directional push toward faster hooks rather than a measured threshold.

cards.title: Match ad type to whether the funnel finishes the sale
cards.summary: Problem-heavy, curiosity-driven ads work when a quiz or landing page continues the sell; simple product ads should instead win on attention and shareability.
cards.use_when: Choosing the creative style (dark problem-solving vs. light meme) for a given product and funnel type.
steps: Decide whether your ad must fully sell or only earn a click. If the ad routes to a quiz, consumption funnel, or strong landing page, the ad only needs to spark curiosity and emotion — do not force a full pitch.

For products with a large emotional problem (e.g., fertility, appearance), lead with the ICP's private fear or self-blame and offer a quiz or next step. Example: 'Stop blaming yourself… take the quiz and see what's stopping you' hits attention, curiosity, emotion, and connection at once.

For lighter, low-emotion products (golf accessories, dip cups, novelty items), win on fast attention and connection: meme formats, jokes, and humor. Example: 'Made for spitters, not quitters' works because it is funny and shareable.
Assess emotion on both ends of the spectrum — positive (humor, laughter) and negative (fear, insecurity) — and pick the one most likely to move your specific buyer, based on your ICP research.
caveats: Examples are the presenter's own client work for DTC brands, not guaranteed results; copy the underlying logic, not the exact lines.

cards.title: Design shareable meme ads that raise AOV
cards.summary: Funny, shareable ad creative lets buyers spread the product and can lift average order value by encouraging friend-to-friend sends.
cards.use_when: Creating acquisition creative for a light-resonance product where you want organic shares or higher basket value.
steps: Identify the in-group identity your buyer wants to signal. For Gen Z / millennial golfers, that meant ads that feel like being 'one of the boys' rather than appealing to the traditional older golfer.
Write in meme language and joke-format copy so the ad itself becomes something the buyer would send to friends. Example: 'the foresome experience you dream about' for golf accessories.
Note the AOV angle: if the ad is shareable and funny, a buyer may forward it, which the presenter ties to increased average order value — treat this as an observed logic, not a guaranteed lift.
Confirm the humor lands with the exact ICP: the same ad should make the target laugh and make an off-target viewer scroll past. Use that two-second test to validate fit before spending.
caveats: The AOV increase is the presenter's observation, not a documented benchmark; test it rather than assuming it.

cards.title: Do days of manual creative research before writing ads
cards.summary: Build a handwritten research document from Reddit, reviews, and comments instead of trusting a five-minute AI research prompt.
cards.use_when: Starting creative production for a new product, niche, or category where you lack buyer language.
steps: Block out three to four consecutive days for manual research on the niche and product before making any ad.
Spend that time inside your customers' real words: Reddit threads, competitor-site reviews, Amazon reviews, TikTok comments, and ad comments.
Build a dedicated research document by manually copying and pasting quotes, reviews, and comments, and taking screenshots — capture raw language, not cleaned-up summaries.
Do not outsource the judgment to AI. As the presenter stresses, a chatbot will not write a funny golf or dipping joke for you; you must find the humor and phrasing yourself from real material.
Use this document as the source of truth for briefs and copy, so ads echo the customer's own voice and in-group slang rather than generic claims.
caveats: The '3–4 days' figure is the presenter's recommendation, scale it to how unfamiliar the niche is; AI can assist in selecting candidates if reviewed by a human.

cards.title: Write creative briefs with six mandatory fields before producing ads
cards.summary: A structured brief (concept, creative type, angle, headline, CTA, visual direction) prevents making 100 copies of one ad.
cards.use_when: Handing off a static ad to a designer or producing it yourself in Canva.
steps: After research, write a brief per ad. Include these fields: (1) Concept, (2) Creative type — curiosity static, us-versus-them, USP callout, social-proof/review, etc. (3) Angle — what you are actually doing and who you are selling to. (4) Headline. (5) CTA. (6) Visual direction.
Always name the creative type explicitly so your set stays diverse and you do not make one hundred near-identical variants.
Use the brief as the production spec: ship it to a designer's attention or review your own brief and build the ad in Canva.
Treat each field as a decision to make deliberately — a missing creative-type or angle field is the fastest route to a monotone, undifferentiated set of ads.
caveats: This is the presenter's own briefing framework; adapt the field list to your team's handoff format.

cards.title: Test ad concepts against a four-question 'made for me' scorecard
cards.summary: A quick checklist confirms an ad speaks to the ICP, opens a curiosity gap, triggers emotion, and shows a path to a solution.
cards.use_when: Pre-launch review of a new creative before you commit spend on Meta.
steps: Score the ad on four points: does it speak directly to the ICP? Does it create a curiosity gap? Does it trigger an emotional response? Does it provide a clear path to a solution?
Use the scorecard to make the viewer feel the ad was made specifically for them — the emotional 'this hits me' reaction, rather than a polished but generic ad.
Kill or rework any ad that looks like everyone else's generic ad or that shows product-spec details nobody cares about, such as t-shirt weight or GSM.
Also test the offer layer alongside the psychology: the presenter admits he often buys purely on a strong offer he cannot refuse — so pair good ad psychology with a compelling offer.
Apply the scorecard before large spend and consider a systematic creative test rather than a single ad slam-dunk.
caveats: The scorecard is a qualitative heuristic from the presenter, not a validated measurement instrument.

06-MEA / measurement and analytics

Goes here. Website and business analytics, measuring organic and paid traffic, Google Analytics, Shopify reporting, root cause analysis frameworks, multi-touch attribution (MTA), post-purchase surveys, marketing mix modeling (MMM), conversion rate optimization (CRO) methodologies, quiz funnel psychology, heatmaps, causal inference methods, incrementality testing, and general marketing/business performance dashboards.

Not here.

Paid advertising performance metrics, ROAS, scaling rules, bidding, or ad-platform specific attribution -> 11-ADC

Financial modeling or accounting -> 20-FIN

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details the rigorous statistical and methodological foundations of A/B testing for e-commerce, outlining sample size math, the dangers of "peeking," Bayesian versus Frequentist models, and a volume-based playbook for scaling experimentation. modules: [MEA] topics: [conversion rate optimization, attribution and modeling, business and marketing analytics] tier: 2 scope_hint: core

Topics. conversion rate optimization / Deconstructing the mathematical realities of A/B testing, emphasizing that true CRO requires evaluating hypotheses under genuine uncertainty rather than running tests to "repair" objectively broken elements. Establishing a stage-gated testing playbook based on monthly order volume, directing low-volume stores (<300 orders/month) to rely on qualitative research and bold, big-swing changes, while reserving complex A/B/n testing, multi-armed bandits, and CUPED variance reduction for high-volume stores (3,000+ orders/month). attribution and modeling / Evaluating the statistical rigor of experimentation by comparing Frequentist models (fixed-horizon) against Bayesian approaches and sequential testing frameworks (mSPRT, GAVI) designed to mitigate the massive false positive risks of "peeking." Outlining critical experiment invalidations—including Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM), flicker (FOOC), and Twyman’s Law—to ensure reported lifts are statistically valid rather than instrumentation artifacts. business and marketing analytics / Navigating platform-specific testing constraints, such as Shopify's deprecation of client-side checkout A/B testing (via checkout extensibility) and the ethical/legal landmines of personalized price testing. Moving away from highly subjective prioritization frameworks (like ICE) toward evidence-gated, profit-weighted models (like PXL) that calculate the true expected value of an experiment before development begins.

Look for. The core mathematical reality of sample size (Evan Miller's formula): detecting a 10% relative lift on a typical 2% baseline requires approximately 80,000 visitors per variant, making micro-tweaks mathematically invalid for most DTC brands. The definition of the "peeking problem": checking A/B test results continuously and stopping as soon as p < 0.05 inflates the false positive rate to over 26%. The definition of Twyman's Law: any figure that looks incredibly interesting or surprising (e.g., a 364% lift) is usually wrong and likely caused by a tracking bug or Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM). The impact of Shopify's checkout extensibility update: it prevents third-party client-side tools from A/B testing the checkout UI, forcing reliance on server-side theme testing (Shopify Rollouts) or Plus-exclusive Checkout Blocks.

Skip. Generic claims about "magic conversion numbers" (e.g., requiring exactly 400 conversions per month to test) that fail to account for Minimum Detectable Effect (MDE) math.

Scope mix. Almost all core.

Volume. 15 to 20.
